items.title: Transporters’ issues almost resolved: Sindh CM
items.description: • Murad Ali Shah directs transport department to address remaining demands • KATI warns prolonged strike could disrupt production, essential supplies • LCCI calls for meaningful dialogue to end strike; says export containers worth $500 million stranded at factories KARACHI: As the goods transporters’ strike entered its sixth day on Thursday, continuing to disrupt industrial activity and exports, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah claimed that the dispute was “almost resolved” and only a few points remained under discussion. Speaking as chief guest at the 79th Independence Day flag-hoisting ceremony organised by the Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) on Thursday, the chief minister directed the provincial transport department to make efforts to settle the remaining issues at the earliest so that disruption facing transporters, industries and businesses could end. A delegation of the Transporters of Goods Association, led by Tariq Gujjar, met the chief minister at the KCCI event, where Mr Shah assured them that their problems would be addressed. On the concerns of Nasla Tower affectees, Mr Shah assured the chamber that the Sindh government would examine the matter, acknowledging that they had suffered serious hardship. He said he would discuss the issue with cabinet members to explore possible solutions. Mr Shah also supported the business community’s ambitious vision of increasing Pakistan’s exports from around $30 billion to $100bn, saying the target was “absolutely achievable” if the country harnessed Sindh’s indigenous energy potential and adopted policies to reduce the cost of doing business and make Pakistani products globally competitive, according to a KCCI press release. He said Pakistan had demonstrated its strength on the defence and diplomatic fronts and “the next battle we have to win is on the economic front”. The chief minister called for unity between the government and business community to achieve sustainable economic growth and strengthen Pakistan’s position in global markets. He said Pakistan had the potential to achieve the $100bn export target, noting that overseas Pakistanis were already sending around $40bn in remittances while exports could rise substantially if competitive policies and a conducive business environment were ensured. Mr Shah said Sindh could become Pakistan’s “energy basket”, with vast Thar coal reserves as well as significant potential in solar, wind and indigenous gas. He maintained that inexpensive electricity generated from domestic resources could reduce production costs, improve industrial competitiveness and enable exporters to compete more effectively in international markets. He particularly stressed the need to fully utilise Thar coal to bring down energy costs, saying Pakistan could not afford to neglect a resource capable of providing relatively inexpensive energy. He also called for greater exploration and utilisation of Sindh’s indigenous gas resources instead of excessive reliance on imported gas. Earlier, Businessmen Group Chairman Zubair Motiwala said Pakistan could increase exports from $30bn to $100bn if the cost of doing business and manufacturing was brought on a par with competing countries. He proposed that the government conduct a comprehensive cost-comparison study of Pakistan and competing economies, including India, Bangladesh and Cambodia, to identify factors making Pakistani products less competitive internationally. Industry sounds alarm Separately, Korangi Association of Trade and Industry (KATI) President Muhammad Ikram Rajput urged the government and transporters to immediately resolve their dispute through negotiations, warning that the prolonged strike was severely disrupting the movement of raw materials, finished products, industrial equipment, essential commodities and other commercial goods. He warned that if the strike continued, disruption in supplies of food and other essential commodities could lead to shortages and higher prices. The suspension of transportation could also disrupt factory production, force some industries to reduce output and cause financial losses, he said. Mr Rajput warned that delays in transporting export consignments to ports could prevent exporters from meeting delivery deadlines, resulting in financial losses, undermining the confidence of foreign buyers and affecting future orders. Meanwhile, the Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) also urged the federal government to end the strike through meaningful dialogue, warning that the prolonged disruption was threatening the supply chain, exports, industrial production and overall economic activity. Expressing concern as the strike entered its sixth consecutive day, LCCI office-bearers led by President Faheemur Rehman Saigol said the deadlock between the government and transporters could have far-reaching consequences for businesses and consumers if not resolved immediately. Mr Saigol said transportation was the backbone of the national economy, connecting manufacturers with markets, ports and consumers, and any prolonged disruption would create pressure across the economic chain. The LCCI urged the government to adopt a pragmatic and conciliatory approach, address the transporters’ genuine concerns and ensure that industrial activity and the movement of essential goods remained uninterrupted. “The textile industry, one of Pakistan’s major export-oriented sectors, has already reported serious disruption,” Mr Saigol said. According to estimates cited by the chamber, export containers worth around $500m were stranded at factories, leaving exporters exposed to missed shipment deadlines, additional demurrage and detention charges and potential claims from international buyers. “The situation is particularly alarming because the textile sector is currently passing through a crucial shipping period. Pakistan cannot afford to lose export orders or damage its credibility with international buyers because of disruptions in domestic logistics,” he said. Khalid Hasnain in Lahore also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: No Adiala visit without confirmation of meeting, says CM Afridi
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Mini­ster Sohail Afridi said on Thursday that he would not visit Adiala jail again before Sept 27 unless the government officially confirmed a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan. He also called for the closure of important government offices, including the Prime Minister’s Off­ice, alleging that they had become dysfunctional. Speaking to the media outside Adiala jail, the KP chief minister said the situation at the prison indicated that the authorities had no intention of allowing him to meet Imran Khan. “I have come to Adiala for the last time before Sept 27. I will return only when the government itself confirms the meeting,” he said. It is worth mentioning that Afridi’s name was also included in the list of people who intended to meet Imran Khan on Thursday. Afridi warned that if the meeting was not allowed, PTI workers would block roads across the country from 10pm on Thursday as part of the party’s “D-Chowk” protest. He urged party workers to prepare to take to the streets carrying national and PTI flags, saying the protest would convey a message that the treatment meted out to the country’s most popular leader since April 2022 was unacceptable. According to PTI media cell, protests were held in different cities. Workers went to the chowks and chanted slogans in favour of Imran Khan. Afridi alleged that even government ministers were acknowledging that the country and its system had been paralysed, claiming that the government had failed. He said the people of Pakistan wanted their issues to be resolved and that this could only be ensured by Imran Khan. He said he would march towards Islamabad on Sept 27 along with two million people. Afridi urged PTI workers and the public to focus on Sept 27, describing the date as a “nightmare” for the authorities. He claimed that people were enthusiastic and that a large number of supporters had gathered in Khyber district at short notice on Wednesday. He said a similar street movement would be launched in other districts and claimed that more than two million people would participate in the Sept 27 mobilisation. He added that a street movement would be held in Bannu on Sunday. He said anyone carrying the flags of Pakistan and PTI would be considered a supporter of Imran Khan. The chief minister’s warning came amid continuing PTI protests and demands for access to its incarcerated founder. The Islamabad High Court has ordered the jail administration to arrange meetings with family members and lawyers on Tuesdays and with party leaders on Thursdays, but the orders have not been implemented for several months. Later in the night, while talking to the media, Afridi said there were orders from three judges allowing meetings with Imran Khan twice a week, but the court orders were not being implemented. “We have filed applications in courts for the implementation of the decisions, but the courts are helpless. In that case, we have every right to hold a protest. Even the prime minister said that he would ask about the meeting and then inform me. If such important offices are dysfunctional, they should be closed as they are consuming public funds. Poor people pay taxes and that money is spent on them,” he said. The KP chief minister said even ministers were saying that the system had collapsed. “Today, labourers, industrialists and all other segments of society have been saying that the country is not going in the right direction. Shehbaz Sharif used to say that if he got 30pc support from the establishment, he would deliver and change the fate of the masses, but he has failed despite getting full support,” he added. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Osun election: Factors that’ll decide Adeleke, Oyebamiji, Salaam, others’ fate tomorrow
items.description: ***Tinubu assures indigenes of adequate security ***15 candidates battle for 1.9m votes By Clifford Ndujihe, Dapo Akinrefon, Henry Umoru & Shina Abubakar OSOGBO — AFTER rounding off their campaigns, yesterday, 15 standard bearers are primed for tomorrow’s governorship election in Osun State. Amid a cloud of tension unfurled by violence and killings that heralded the campaigns, President Bola Tinubu, yesterday, assured people of the state adequate security during and after polls and urged them to troop out en masse to exercise their franchise. No fewer than 1.9m of 2,339,233 registered voters who collected PVCs across 30 local government areas, 323 wards, and 3,763 polling units are expected to decide the fate of candidates led by Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord seeking re-election, Bola Oyebamiji of the All Progressives Congress, APC; and Najeem Salaam of the African Democratic Congress, ADC. Factors such as influence of critical stakeholders and leaders, popularity, performance, incumbency, federal might and track record among others are expected to shape the outcome of the balloting. Meanwhile, fresh violence erupted in Ijesaland, yesterday, as some suspected political hoodlums stormed Esa-Oke, and shot two members of the APC. The victims are Oladele Ayegbo and Taiwo Oluwatobi. They however, said that the attack happened on Wednesday as security agencies embarked on show force in the state in readiness for the election. Already15,000 policemen, 31 Commissioners of Police, helicopters, and drones have been deployed. Disturbed by the circle of violence, the Amnesty International Nigeria has vowed to make Senator Francis Fadahunsi an example in its campaign against impunity and inflammatory rhetoric by politicians, following remarks attributed to him in a viral video ahead of the poll. Also, former Chief of Defence Staff, General Lucky Irabor (retd), has called for decisive action, including arrest against politicians and other prominent Nigerians who make inciting statements capable of triggering violence and disrupting the peace of the country. Tinubu’s assurance Ahead of the poll, President Tinubu has assured the people of adequate security during and after the exercise. Tinubu gave the promise during the grand finale of the governorship campaign of the APC held in Osogbo, the Osun State capital yesterday to formally present its candidate, Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, for the Saturday election. Represented by President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, Tinubu said: “Let me assure all Osun indigenes that adequate security has been provided all over the state to ensure people come out to cast their votes for the candidate of their choice without any fear or intimidation. Feel very free to cast your votes for the candidate of your choice.” The candidates, their strengths, weaknesses With less than two days to the governorship election in Osun State and the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, confirming that 2,339, 233 residents registered to participate in the polls, candidates and political parties are rounding up campaigns and intensifying moves to warm themselves into the hearts of the people with a view to winning their support to emerge as the next governor of the state. Of the 15 political parties and their candidates listed by INEC for the August 15 governorship polls, the most visible candidates have presented their manifestoes, gone beyond consultation and round up campaigns across the local government areas. Candidates and their parties Candidates in the race include Governor Ademola Adeleke (Accord party), Farinloye Olanrewaju (Action Alliance), Esan Olajide (African Action Congress, AAC); Najeem Salaam (ADC); Adeagbo Opawoye (African Democratic Party, ADP), Mustapha Adeniyi, Social Democratic Party, (SDP) and Bola Oyebamiji ( APC). Others are Adesina Aseyemi-Doro (All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA); Adewale Adebayo (Allied People Movement, APM); Clement Adesuyi (Action Peoples Party, APP); Masilo Adeleke (Boot Party); Taofeek Adeleke (New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP); Saliu Oyelami (Peoples Redemption Party, PRP), Ogunsakin Olalekan (Young Progressives Party, YPP) and Adefemi Adesuyi (Zenith Labour Party, ZLP). Out of the 15 candidates, three have emerged as front-runners of which Governor Adeleke hinged his re-election campaign on his five-point agenda reloaded. Mr Bola Oyebamiji of APC, tagged his manifesto as ‘Prosperity agenda’ and Najeem Salaam of the ADC launched a 10-point agenda. Adeleke’s prospects Apart from being the incumbent governor, he also enjoys acceptability among the majority of civil servants and the leadership of the labour unions. The NLC, TUC and JNC are all on his side and appeared in the Accord party campaigns soliciting support for the governor. The governor is also banking on his achievements in the area of infrastructure across the three senatorial districts. In addition, the Ede-born politician seems to be enjoying the backing of some traditional rulers in the state, led by the Ataoja of Osogbo, who on different occasions publicly declared support for the governor and Accord party despite resistance from his subjects. Also, Adeleke is said to enjoy the support of his former party, the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, through which he won the governorship poll about four years ago.and a section of the Labour Party, LP The PDP’s failure to field a candidate for the 2026 polls in the state is more of an advantage for the governor’s re-election bid as the party’s structure, apart from a few strong men, still works for Accord. Omisore’s loyalists’ defection Another major advantage the governor has is the defection of Senator Iyiola Omisore’s loyalists to Accord Party due to the fallout of the APC primaries. Although, Omisore did not leave the APC, many of his associates who served in the Gboyega Oyetola administration, including three commissioners and special advisers, left the party and joined Accord. He is a strong factor in the Ife axis. It is also believed that Governor Adeleke has an advantage in Osun-West Senatorial District, where he won massively in 2022. Interestingly, the APC candidate is also from the district, which is expected to deepen the battle for votes in Osun West. Ede federal constituency, which the Governor hails from, consisting of Ede-North, Ede-South, Egbedore and Ejigbo local governments, has a total of 319,489 registered voters. This is a major advantage for the governor who still retains a hold on the area. Besides, some bigwigs like Ibukun Fadipe, Sunday Bisi, Disu Babatunde among others may swing votes in Adeleke’s favour in Ijesaland. In Osun Central, the governor enjoy the support of the Ataoja of Osogbo, Secretary to the State Government, Teslim Igbalaye, Mr Gani Ola-Oluwa and the House of Representatives member, Mr Morufu Adewale, who are likely to help the governor’s cause in Osogbo and Olorunda local government. Challenges The governor’s major problems stem from policy decisions early in his administration. The opposition cites the sacking of teachers and health workers without replacements; sacking of media workers at the state-owned broadcast stations and the administration’s failure to recruit civil servants as a minus for his re-election bid. The administration is facing allegation of nepotism, with outcry over recent employment into the teaching service and the University of Ilesa favouring Ede indigenes and shutting out other towns. Also, the governor’s performance in major sectors like agriculture, health, commerce, industry and education form major issues for his opponents’ campaign strategies. Another factor that may affect the fortunes of the governor is that a major PDP bloc loyal to former governor, Olagunsoye Oyinlola has publicly dumped the governor for the candidate of the APM, Mr Adewale Adebayo. Oyebamiji’s prospects The APC candidate, whose personality and philanthropy have endeared him to the people, is believed to enjoy the support of President Tinubu and APC governors. Apart from being endorsed by the President, Oyebamiji’s election bid received a major boost with the defection of all the federal lawmakers from Osun-East senatorial district, who are also major political gladiators from the towns. They include Senator Francis Fadahunsi, Mr Wole Oke (Ijesa-North federal constituency), Sanya Omirin (Ijesa-South federal constituency) and Mr Taofeek Ajilesoro (Ife federal constituency). Besides, some of Omisore’s point men in Ife have also pledged loyalty to the party and its candidate. While Adeleke got massive votes from Osun-West in 2022, the candidature of Oyebamiji may change the narrative, with the total registered votes from Ikire federal constituency amounting to 222,786 votes for Irewole, Ayedaade and Isokan local governments, likely reducing the influence of the governor in the district. While Governor Adeleke seems to enjoy endorsement of royal fathers from Ife, Oyebamiji’s major endorsement has been coming from markets and traders. In most of his engagements, the APC candidate took advantage of the allegation of nepotism against the incumbent to sell himself as a man for all and inaugurated 30 vote canvassers for each of the 3,763 polling units across the state. Oyebamiji is likely to win in Osun-East due to the presence of Senator Francis Fadahunsi, a major political gladiator from Ijesaland, Hon Sanya Omirin and Wole Oke from Ijesa-South and North respectively. Although, Senator Iyiola Omisore is still a member of the APC, some of his loyalists are still within the party. Also Engr. Kayode Adereti, the deputy governorship candidate of the party, is influential, having contested against incumbent member of the House of Representatives in 2022 – Taofeek Ajilesoro, who is now also in the APC. In Osun-Central, whoever wins in Osogbo and Olorunda local government is likely to win the senatorial district. Oyebamiji has the likes of the party’s national secretary, Senator Ajibola Basiru who is from core Osogbo supported by Executive Director, Marine and Blue Economy, Olalekan Badmus and many elites in the Olorunda and Osogbo, supporting the APC. Challenges Oyebamiji’s major issue is the policy decision of the Oyetola administration under whom he served. The modulated salary under Governor Rauf Aregbesola and the inability of Governor Gboyega Oyetola to pay part of it has been a major issue confronting his candidature. His critics, especially from the Accord party, believe he is responsible for the modulated salary under Aregbesola’s administration and should not be trusted with the governorship seat. Najeem Salaam’s prospects Since unveiling his 10 point agenda, anchored on workers’ welfare and sustainable electricity for industrialisation of the state, Salaam, a former Speaker of the House of Assembly, has continuously engaged with the electorate on the need to abandon the traditional political parties. Salaam’s advantage is Aregbesola’s grassroots appeal when he was governor in the state and the candidate’s humble nature that attracts him to a section of supporters across the state, especially from Osun-West Senatorial District where he hails from. Many grassroots politicians, who left the APC along with Aregbesola, are with Salaam. His Osun-West senatorial district roots can harm both Adeleke and Oyebamiji, and could be an advantage should he decide to go into an alliance work with either of the two. He has, however, vowed to reach the finish line as he claims to be better qualified to govern the state than any of the candidates. Ogbeni Aregbesola’s influence in Osogbo and Ilesa East local government may also work for Salaam’s ambition. His challenges Salaam’s major challenge is his affiliation with Rauf Aregbesola, who is National Secretary of the ADC. Civil servants are yet to forgive the former governor, who had bitter experiences with the modulated salary and pension issues during Aregbesola’s tenure. Observers of political events in the state posit that the ADC does not have the necessary state-wide structure needed to prosecute an election, and the needed resources to run a successful governorship project. The three major candidates are from Osun-West Senatorial District, hence the district is going to be a battleground with Adeleke coming from Ede-North and Ede-South; Oyebamij from Irewole local government and Salaam is from Ejigbo local government area of the state. LG crisis Another important factor is control of the grassroots, local government administration is said to be the closest to the local people and the Accord and APC battled extensively for control which is yet to be resolved as the matter is still a subject of litigation. However, in the meantime the APC is still “controversially” in control of Local Government in the state. Infrastructure development A major factor is the infrastructure drive in the state in the last three and half years, the Governor Adeleke-led administration said it has completed over 300 km of road network across the State, including many first, such as the first dualised roads in Ilesa, Iwo, Ede and Ila-Orangun. The people applauded the governor for the feat achieved. Elite conspiracy One of the issues going into the polls is the elite conspiracy against the governor’s immediate family members. The governor may not really have problems with the Osun elite, but the way his immediate family, especially his elder sister, allegedly runs the affairs of government behind the scenes does not go well with them. Many classified the administration as the Adeleke dynasty government rather than one run by party or state stakeholders. This formed part of the reason many political gladiators like Senator Francis Fadahunsi, Mr Wole Oke, Prince Olagunsoye Oyinlola, Alhaji Shuaib Oyedokun among others parted ways with the governor. Single-term syndrome Since the creation of Osun State, those elected as governor, apart from Aregbesola, served only one term in office. It is to be seen if Adeleke will get a second term like Aregbesola. Traditional rulers This election has divided traditional rulers along party lines. While others simply chose to support their subject, the Timi of Ede, Oba Adesola Lawal, openly campaigned for the Accord and the governor. He publicly disclosed that Ede indigenes should vote for Accord to retain power in the town. Also, the Akire and other traditional rulers in Irewole federal constituency have endorsed Oyebamiji, saying the constituency will prefer to have their son on the seat of power as means to guarantee their growth and development. While the Ataoja of Osogbo, Oba Jimoh Oyetunji has thrown his weight behind Governor Adeleke over what Adeleke has done in the town, the Oluwo of Iwo, Oba Abdurosheed Akanbi is backing the APC. The Oluwo has openly told monarchs from Iwoland not to go the wrong way during the election on Saturday. However, the Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Ogunwusi has retained his status of father to all, separating the palace from party politics. Oyinlola backing Oyebamiji Former Osun State governor, Prince Olagunsoye Oyinlola has pitched his tent with Oyebamiji and has promised to mobilize for the victory of the APC candidate. Oyinlola, a chieftain of the PDP, who announced his support for Oyebamiji, said Osun requires a different direction. Several political leaders from the PDP and other political structures had also thrown their weight behind Oyebamiji, including former senator Olasunkanmi Akinlabi, former secretary to the Osun state government Fatai Akinbade and former PDP national vice-chairman Tajudeen Oladipo. Omisore’s support In the 2018 governorship election, Senator Iyiola Omisore, who was also contesting the governorship race, supported Oyetola during the supplementary elections to defeat Adeleke. Omisore’s looming image helped Oyetola get 28,000 votes to beat Adeleke. In the Ile-Ife axis, Omisore is seen as a power bloc, whose support base is capable of swinging the votes in favour of Oyebamiji. Though during the electioneering campaigns, Omisore was conspicuously absent due to his being allegedly sidelined, however, a meeting with President Tinubu a fortnight ago made him change his mind to support Oyebamiji. APC’s campaign DG killed 2days to election Meanwhile, few hours to the election, fresh violence has erupted in Ijesaland as some suspected political hoodlums stormed Esa-Oke, and shot two APC members – Oladele Ayegbo and Taiwo Oluwatobi. Oladele Ayegbo, a nephew of the APC campaign council Director-General, Mr Wole Oke, was reported to have died on the spot while the second victim, Oluwatobi is recuperating at the hospital. The APC campaign council Media Committee Chairman, Remi Omowaye while addressing newsmen yesterday, said three other persons were attacked in Ilesa same day while one of its House of Representatives candidates, Francis Eniade was attacked inside police station at Okuku by hoodlums working for a governorship candidate. “The APC was not accusing the police of complicity but urged the security agency to act swiftly and decisively in line with its constitutional responsibility to protect lives and property as the state prepares for Saturday’s governorship election,” he said. In a statement issued on Thursday, Osun APC spokesperson Kola Olabisi revealed that Ayegbo was killed on Wednesday night near his residence in the Idofin area of Esa-Oke, located in the Obokun Local Government Area. According to the party, suspected hoodlums operating from a vehicle carried out the attack. “The Osun State chapter of the APC has condemned the killing of the party’s governorship campaign Director-General, Wole Oke’s nephew, Dele Ayegbo, in Esa-Oke, Obokun Local Government Area of the state on Wednesday night by the hit squad of the Accord party who have been terrorising the members and supporters of the opposition APC across the state,” the statement reads. “Information has it that Ayegbo was gunned down at the road junction close to his house at the Idofin quarters area of the ancient town by the Accord Party hoodlums who were riding in a car.” Olabisi stated that two party members were targeted in the shooting. While Ayegbo died instantly at the scene, the second victim sustained gunshot wounds and was rushed to an undisclosed local hospital for medical treatment. Attack happened on Wednesday —Police When contacted, Police Public Relations Officer, Osun Command, DSP Abiodun Ojelabi confirmed the incident, saying the attack was carried out on Wednesday night around 11pm. Ojelabi said: “One Oladele Ayegbo has passed away while the other victim is receiving treatment at the hospital. More police unit have been deployed to the area to assist the Division to secure the town more appropriately,” he said. 15,000 policemen, 31 CPs deployed To police the poll, the Force Public Relations Officer, Anietie Iniedu said the Police have deployed 15,000 policemen and 31 Commissioners of Police to oversee each local government during the exercise. He added that police helicopter and drone unit have also been deployed to conduct aerial surveillance before, during and immediately after the election on Saturday. His words: “We have 15,000 police officers on the ground, drawn from several combat and tactical units; the PMF, the TAPU, the Bomb Squad and the Special Protection Unit. We also have men from our tactical units on the ground. We have men on patrol, and we have men stationed at strategic locations. “As I speak to you, we have deployed one unit of armed mobile police officers to every local government area. So, we have 30 units across the local government areas. A unit is actually about 60 police officers, including 50 armed police officers. So, we have a unit for each local government area. “The men posted to the local government areas are being coordinated by a Commissioner of Police. There is a Commissioner of Police in each local government area. We also have a Deputy Commissioner of Police in each local government area, as well as a Mobile Police Commander and a PMF Commander in each local government area”, he said. INEC office CSP Iniedu further disclosed that two units of armed mobile policemen were attached to the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, headquarters in the state to ensure adequate security “We also have two units of armed mobile police officers attached to the Independent National Electoral Commission headquarters in Osogbo. We have two units of armed police officers posted there. Helicopters, drones deployed “As of today, our helicopter and drone units have arrived in Osogbo, and they will be conducting area surveillance from now, during and immediately after the election”, he added. Security agencies embark on show of force The security agencies, including Police, DSS, Army, Air Force, NSCDC personnel among others have been going round for show of force to deter criminal-minded people from engaging in activities that may disrupt the peace and harmony of the state ahead of the poll. He also disclosed that the state will be locked down from 12am on Saturday till after the election and only essential workers, and voters will be allowed to move around throughout election period. “The Army is cordoning all border roads leading into Osun State. And so, by 12 a.m. on Saturday, we will be locking down the state. We will not be allowing any vehicular movement apart from those on essential duty, security duties and those going to cast their franchise”. ‘We’ll use Fadahunsi as example’ – Amnesty vows Amnesty International Nigeria has vowed to make Senator Francis Fadahunsi an example in its campaign against impunity and inflammatory rhetoric by politicians, following remarks attributed to him in a viral video ahead of Saturday’s governorship election in Osun State. In the video, Fadahunsi, who represents Osun East Senatorial District, was alleged to have directed his supporters to “kill” members of the Accord Party, which has incumbent Governor Adeleke as its governorship candidate. The senator has, however, denied making any call for physical attacks, insisting that the viral video was edited to distort the meaning of his comment. Speaking on Channels Television’s Sunrise Daily on Thursday, Country Director of Amnesty International Nigeria, Isa Sanusi, condemned the remarks attributed to Fadahunsi and said the organisation would use the case to challenge what he described as impunity among Nigerian politicians. “We are going to use him as an example because this is the first time. We had so many other terrible politicians say terrible things ahead of elections, but this one is exceptional. A situation whereby somebody came out on record saying ‘kill them wherever you find them’, I believe that that person does not deserve any peace again because advocacy of hatred is a crime under international law as well as Nigerian laws. “Therefore, we are going to use this man as an example to show that the impunity by Nigerian politicians cannot continue and we cannot tolerate it again; the people have to hold them to account if the government could not do that,” Sanusi said. People who make inciting statements should be arrested – Ex-CDS Irabor In like manner, former Chief of Defence Staff, General LEO Irabor(retd), has called for decisive action, including arrest, against politicians and other prominent Nigerians who make inciting statements capable of triggering violence and disrupting the peace of the country. Speaking on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, Irabor condemned Senator Fadahunsi’s statement and commended the police for questioning him. “For me as a person, any time we hear individuals who make inciting comments, I think that such people should be picked up immediately, and that is why I am glad that even though the statement made by Senator Fadahunsi is a political one, but I think that it also borders on incitement to violence. I think the police have done the right thing by inviting him, and he should be questioned even beyond that,” General Irabor said. The former Defence chief also called for the arrest of Islamic clerics Sani Jingir and Ahmad Gumi over what he described as inciting statements they had made at different times. “Added to that is of course the Sheik in Kano, Sheik Jingir, who also made some comments which of course I believe is also inciting that could also add to the bouquet of threats that we have, he also should be arrested and I also believe that the various comments that someone like Gumi has been making also demands that he be called not just to order but of course invited and arrested in other to let the populace know that there is nobody who is above the law and then when you say things that are not right you should be called in to answer,” the former service chief said. Let people choose, peace must prevail — Obi Also, Presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr. Peter Obi has called on all stakeholders in Saturday’s Osun State governorship election to ensure that voters are allowed to exercise their franchise freely and without intimidation. Obi made the call in a statement posted on his X platform, yesterday, urging the INEC, security agencies, political parties, candidates and other stakeholders to maintain neutrality, professionalism and restraint before, during and after the election. The former Anambra State governor said the people of Osun State must be allowed to determine their leaders through a transparent and credible electoral process. He urged INEC to ensure that votes were properly counted, protected and announced in accordance with the wishes of the electorate. “Osun belongs to its people. Therefore, I call on the Independent National Electoral Commission, security agencies, political parties, candidates, government institutions, civil society organisations, religious and traditional leaders, the media, and every stakeholder to act with the highest degree of neutrality, professionalism, and restraint,” Obi said. He appealed to residents of Osun to reject violence and resist attempts by politicians to create divisions within communities for electoral advantage. “To those within Osun State, I appeal for peace. Do not allow politicians to turn your neighbours, friends, and communities against each other. Do not destroy your state in the name of winning an election,” he said. Obi also called on politicians, supporters, influencers and financiers outside the state to avoid actions that could fuel violence or intimidation during the poll. He specifically urged security agencies to remain loyal to the Constitution and the Nigerian state rather than political parties or individuals. Obi appealed to the international community, diplomatic missions and election observers to closely monitor the election, saying their presence could strengthen public confidence in Nigeria’s democratic process. Sensitive materials arrive Osogbo Meanwhile, INEC sensitive materials arrived Osogba, late yesterday, ahead of tomorrow’s poll. Osun AG sues IGP, seeks order compelling police to probe Fadahunsi The Osun State Government has approached a state high sitting in Osogbo, seeking an order compelling the police to investigate Senator Francis Fadahunsi over alleged inflammatory remarks and threats against members and supporters of the Accord Party ahead of Saturday’s governorship election. The suit, filed by the state Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Oluwole Jimi-Bada, SAN, seeks an Order of Mandamus against the Inspector-General of Police and Commissioner of Police, Osun State Command. Fadahunsi, who represents Osun East senatorial district, was joined in the suit as the person affected or interested party. The government said the action followed a video circulating on social media, allegedly showing Fadahunsi addressing a political gathering in front of the Owa Obokun’s Palace, Ilesha, on August 11, 2026. According to court documents, the senator allegedly made remarks interpreted as calls for violence against Accord party members, including directing supporters to attack them wherever they were found. The government alleged that Fadahunsi also threatened their families, directed supporters to chase Accord members from hotels and made derogatory comments about the party’s yellow caps. It further alleged that the senator threatened that the election would not hold if Accord members resisted the alleged actions of APC supporters. The state is asking the court to compel the police to investigate the video and determine whether the alleged statements constitute criminal offences. It also wants the police to preserve, authenticate and conduct forensic examination of the complete video to establish whether it had been altered or edited. Other reliefs sought include an order directing the police to take preventive measures to protect Accord candidates, members and voters from intimidation and harassment before, during and after the election. In a supporting affidavit, Nurudeen Kareem, Special Adviser to Governor Ademola Adeleke on Legal Matters, said Accord members had expressed “reasonable and legitimate concerns regarding their safety and security before, during, and after the forthcoming election.” The government argued that the police had a statutory responsibility under the Police Act 2020 and the 1999 Constitution to prevent crime and maintain public order. It said: “The applicant believes that waiting until actual violence, deaths, or injuries occur before investigating an alleged public instruction to kill political opponents would amount to a dereliction of duty.” The Attorney-General stressed that the suit was not asking the court to determine Fadahunsi’s guilt, but to compel the police to perform their statutory duties and take appropriate preventive action. With the election scheduled for Saturday, the government said “time is of the absolute essence,” warning that failure to act on the alleged threat could have serious consequences for public safety and the electoral process. The post Osun election: Factors that’ll decide Adeleke, Oyebamiji, Salaam, others’ fate tomorrow appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Coalition buys time on judges, but harder questions persist
items.description: WHILE it seems that the deadlock over judges’ appointments has been resolved for now, there are still many sticking points souring ties between the PML-N and PPP, which would have to be addressed in the days to come, Dawn has learnt. The bad blood from recriminations over the conduct of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir had hardly settled when the two ruling allies found themselves in a standoff over the appointment of high court judges, nominated by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP). The matter, which was finally resolved on Tuesday after being delayed for several weeks, is just one of the many bumps on the road for the two coalition partners, who have recently found themselves at odds over three major issues — AJK elections, the appointments of new judges, and the reopening of a debate on new provinces. In background discussions, leaders from both parties told Dawn that while the PPP is looking to their leadership for guidance on how to proceed under the circumstances, the PML-N may prefer to defer discussion on sensitive issues — especially the question of new provinces — for as long as possible, lest it derail the coalition’s ‘marital bliss’, so to speak. PPP insiders say party still mulling course of action; PML-N wants to leave ‘touchy subject’ of new provinces for next assembly to tackle On Monday night, a crucial meeting was held in Parliament House to settle the judges’ issue. In attendance was President Asif Ali Zar­dari’s legal team, including his legal adviser Irfan Qadir, Sindh Law Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar and Karachi Mayor Barrister Murtaza Wahab. Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, meanwhile, was the sole representative from the government’s side. Arranged by the National Assembly Secretariat, the meeting was held on a single-point agenda, i.e. the delayed notification of high court judges, a source privy to the meeting told Dawn. Earlier reports had indicated that the president’s legal team had objected to the JCP proceedings, noting that nearly all PPP nominees had been rejected, and that some of the recommended candidates even had criminal records. While the government had been considering the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to bypass the need for presidential approval of the decision, the option became less attractive after the Islamabad High Court took up the matter and issued notices to all parties concerned. With the matter becoming sub judice, both sides felt it was more prudent to settle the matter ‘out of court’, leading to Monday’s confab that finally broke the deadlock over the JCP-sanctioned appointments. A senior PPP office-bearer told Dawn that the meeting with the government and President Zardari’s subsequent assent for the judicial appointments were meant to avoid any adverse decision from the court. However, with around a couple of dozen judicial vacancies still to be filled, insiders say it is ext­remely likely that some PPP nominees will be accommodated in the next round of appointments. According to the PPP leader, the government side had assured the party that in the future, all major decisions will be taken after consultation. However, such promises have been made and broken in the past as well. Future of the coalition? When asked about the future of the coalition partnership, the leader said that barring some political skirmishes — which were par for the course — the alliance between the two parties would continue. However, the PPP office-bearer was adamant that his party would not defend any unconstitutional move, whether regarding the creation of new provinces, or any other issue. Talking to Dawn , another party leader from Karachi said that while the Presidency had broken the ice with the PML-N, party leaders are still waiting for guidance from Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on how to proceed. When asked about the thinking behind the Presidency’s relenting on the issue of judges, the party leader said that while Mr Zardari believed in the “politics of reconciliation” and was “always willing to give others some space”, his son’s stance is usually quite tough. “He does not settle for less,” the PPP leader said of Bilawal’s approach, adding: “That is why I am saying that the party’s direction on its relationship with the government will be determined by the chairman’s actions or statements, and not by the party’s response to any move initiated by the government”. The source said they expected a meeting of the PPP’s Central Executive Committee to be convened very soon, as there were several outstanding issues that warranted discussion at that forum — from the recently-strained relations with the government in the Centre to the fresh debate over new provinces or administrative units. “I think a CEC meeting would be called soon, maybe shortly after August 14. The party ranks also need clarity on several issues… [and] everyone looks towards chairman [Bilawal] for direction and policy,” he added. New provinces ‘off the table’ The PML-N, meanwhile, has also been mulling the aggressive stance adopted by the PPP on certain issues, and if the grapevine is to be believed, the party would prefer to defer discussion on these touchy subjects for as long as possible. A party leader close to the Sharif family told Dawn that the PPP was far more concerned about the proposal for new provinces, and the pressure being exerted by “the powers that be” in this regard. “President Zardari must have sought some assurances from the prime minister on this matter before agreeing to the judges’ appointments,” he said. The insider said that a proposal had been floated by the PML-N leadership that the question of creating new administrative units should be deferred for now, and placed before the next National Assembly and provincial assemblies, which would be elected in 2029. “Until then, the PML-N wants the proposal to remain off the table,” he added. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Govt raises petrol price by Rs0.45, high-speed diesel by Rs1.16
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Thursday raised the price of petrol by Rs0.45 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.16. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs325.43 per litre while HSD will cost Rs383.95 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable for August 14 (Friday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: The unfinished independence
items.description: EVERY August, we raise the flag and call ourselves free. But on the first morning of that freedom, in 1947, Faiz, in Subh-i-Azadi , looked at the long-awaited dawn and said it was not the one: ‘yeh da agh daagh ujala, yeh shab-gazida sehar ’ — this stained, night-bitten dawn is not the morning we had set out for. Seventy-nine years on, our national day deserves an honest question: did we win a country and quietly postpone its freedom? In 1947, we changed the nationality of our rulers and left the harder task — changing the nature of rule — to a later generation. That is our unfinished independence — still ours to finish. Begin with the one thing the British empire left behind that no repeal can reach: not a law, but a habit of mind. Colonial rule does not merely occupy a land; it occupies the imagination of those it governs, teaching them to see themselves through the ruler’s eyes — as subjects to be managed, not citizens to be served; supplicants at a counter, not owners of the state. Ashis Nandy called colonialism, above all, a colonisation of the mind — a condition that outlives the flag. This servility was not an accident of empire; it was its design. In 1835, Lord Macaulay told the British that education in India should produce a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect — trained not to rule but to serve. That reflex — to defer, to request rather than require, to treat power as something that happens to us rather than something that belongs to us — is the empire’s most durable export. A new nation needs strong institutions to hold power to account — parties with roots, a parliament with nerve. We did not yet have them: our leadership was thin and soon thinned further, our parties young and quarrelsome. India inherited a mass movement decades in the making and gave itself a constitution within three years. We took nine — nine years without the rules of a shared game, which are exactly the years in which a political culture is meant to grow. Into that vacuum stepped the two institutions the empire had built to their fullest strength — the army and the civil service, disciplined and sure of themselves while everything else improvised. The old colonial master had sailed home; a new establishment, home-grown but colonial in instinct, took his chair. That is the quiet tragedy of our first independence: we did not defeat colonialism so much as change its address. How do we raise citizens — and judges — with the strength to say no when power sits across the table offering everything? And here I must speak of my own house, for the gravest damage was done not by generals or bureaucrats but by judges. The judiciary was meant to be the citizen’s shield — the one institution whose purpose is to say no to power on the authority of law. But it too was a colonial inheritance, and carried the reflex in its bones: under the Raj it had served the sovereign, not the subject, and at independence it transferred that loyalty from the departed Crown to the new establishment, not the people. So when the tanks rolled, the courts, again and again, said yes. They fashioned a doctrine of necessity to legalise the seizure of power; they swore in usurpers; they dressed lawlessness in the robes of law. The colonial mind inside the judiciary has cost this country more than any single dictator, for it turned the guardian of the Constitution into the notary of its breach. Why did they give in? For three human reasons that have nothing to do with law. The first is fear: independence has cost judges their careers, their liberty, at times their lives. The second, and the least confessed, is comfort — the office, the title, the house and the car. The third is isolation — the weight of standing alone when colleagues have already found reasons to look away. What resists them is the one thing a law degree does not issue: character. So the question for our second independence is disarmingly simple: how do we raise citizens — and judges — with the strength to say no when power sits across the table, speaking softly and offering everything? Here I have reached a conviction that may sound strange: that strength is not built by law. It is built by the humanities. History dismantles the oldest alibi of every surrender — the plea that ‘these times are unprecedented’ and so exempt from principle; whoever knows history has heard that lie before, and knows how it ends. Philosophy teaches us to reason about ends, not merely means. Literature is our only sustained practice at inhabiting another human being, without which justice is merely filing. That is why the second independence will begin not in a courtroom or a parliament but in a classroom. If we want judges who will not sign the unjust order, we must form them long before they reach the bench — students given not only the mechanics of the law but a settled conviction about what the Constitution is for. The student of conviction becomes the honest lawyer; the honest lawyer, the fearless bar leader; the fearless bar leader, the judge who says no. Give a generation that conviction and no amendment can take it from them, for a conviction cannot be amended. Pakistan was dreamed by a poet and argued into being by a lawyer — Iqbal’s conviction, Jinnah’s case. Somewhere we kept the lawyer and forgot the poet, and were left with arguments but no convictions. This Independence Day, let us call the poet back — into our schools, our courts, and our idea of what an educated citizen owes his country. The dawn Faiz described is still stained. He told us to keep walking — ‘ chale chalo ’ — for the true morning has not yet come. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He is currently the Distinguished Chair in Constitutionalism & Justice and Professor of Practice at the Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, Lums. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Crime and punishment
items.description: OVER the last few months, I’ve observed this scene many times around Lahore. At a crossroads, the traffic lights are out, have been switched off or are blinking on yellow; the traffic is a mess, and though there are three to four traffic police officers standing on one side, they are not even trying to manage the traffic flow. Instead, they are only interested in stopping and fining motorcyclists and drivers of commercial vehicles. Is ensuring a smooth traffic flow not part of traffic policemen’s responsibility? Is making money for the state (or themselves) their primary function, or is ensuring safety for all through implementing a rules-based traffic flow their primary duty? One of the first principles we teach in economics is that ‘people respond to incentives’. If the traffic wardens are more concerned about making money and meeting their quotas for traffic challans, clearly, these are incentives that have been set by the state and officers are simply responding to them. The traffic department’s message seems to be that meeting quotas and raising a certain amount from challans is more important than making sure that the traffic moves safely and freely. Is this the way to ensure better compliance? Will this lead to better traffic flows in the future? Challans and fines were meant to help ensure safety and smooth traffic on the roads, but they seem to have become an end unto themselves! I doubt the current traffic department managers are really thinking about the medium- or long-term impact of the policy they seem to be following. But the turn to severe punitive measures as a means of ensuring compliance seems to be a more general turn that officials of almost all state departments have resorted to in Pakistan. We are caught in a vicious cycle where compliance in the short term has become an important variable and departments have learnt that the way to achieving better compliance is by upping the ante and making the punishment more severe. A lot of departments seem to be following the same pattern now. The use of the stick over the long term will have some unintended consequences. When increasing fines to deter fast driving on motorways was not seen to be effective, the punishment was enhanced with the registration of FIRs and even arresting those breaking the law. We know our legal system well. An FIR against an individual can mean years of entanglement with the legal system and significant time, money and other costs. But does the punishment fit the crime anymore? Has registering FIRs had the desired impact in terms of deterrence? If not, why was it done? If it did have an impact, is it still fair punishment for driving at 150 kilometres per hour or more on the motorway when the legal limit is 120 km? This has also happened to young motorcyclists without proper documentation. FIRs were registered against them and some 16-18-year-olds were even arrested. FIRs can ruin any young person’s future and career. Entanglements with the legal system can derail educational and career plans. Eventually, the political leadership had to step in and show magnanimity and let off some of the young people. But the trend is clear. Steep fines and/or arrests can happen if your utility provider feels that you have been stealing gas or electricity or have tampered with the meter. Tax authorities have been given significant powers as well. A tweet, perceived to be against important national institutions, personnel, or the national interest can mean not only notices from law-enforcement agencies, but also years of prosecution and imprisonment. News reporting has become a lot more dangerous now. Punitive action can be taken through new laws that have been enacted to curb speech; in fact, closing down programmes or channels and/or getting individual journalists fired can also be achieved through informal means. HRCP has expressed serious concerns about the way in which Punjab’s crime control and terrorism control departments have been handling suspects: there have been far too many deaths in alleged encounters and almost no judicial inquiries have followed. The concerned departments have, of course, denied any wrongdoing but the number of incidents, compared to past records and to what has been happening in other jurisdictions, raises serious questions about extrajudicial actions. It seems the game is about the short term. In the short term, compliance will definitely respond to harsher punishment (the stick), especially if the latter is isolating and does not give the recipients the time and space to mount an institutional response or elicit a reaction from institutions that should be providing a means of balance and/or appeal. The pendulum is swinging in one direction right now. But the problem with the use of the stick is that it is harder to make it sustainable and it will, for sure, have some unintended consequences. The harsher punishment will become the norm and the new baseline. To keep deterrence effective, the departments will have to keep making punishment harsher. If the punishment is harsh now, it will be even more out of sync with the nature of the crime when it is enhanced. What happens to citizens’ trust in the state, their expectation of fair and just treatment and communitarian development and their sentiments about their future in the country and the future of the country itself? Countries are not made for harsh laws and punitive implementation. They are run with trust and mutual benefits and joint gains. The punitive trend has weakened the larger purpose and will continue to do so. The short term might look good right now, but it will undermine where we want to go in the medium to long term. Individual departments and officers might be too blinkered to see this, but the political leadership should be able to read the situation and correct course. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Petroleum levy collection hits record Rs1.57tr
items.description: • Cost of running civil govt rises 16pc, crosses Rs1tr for first time • Fiscal deficit shrinks to 2.6pc on the back of provincial surpluses, lower interest bill • Defence spending up 18pc; primary surplus reaches record 2.9pc of GDP ISLAMABAD: With a record Rs1.567 trillion petroleum levy collection amid record consumer-end oil prices following US-Israel attacks on Iran, the cost of running the civil government rose 16 per cent in the fiscal year 2025-26 to cross Rs1tr for the first time despite restructuring and austerity measures, official data showed on Thursday. At the same time, record cash surpluses from the provinces and a sharp fall in interest payments helped contain the fiscal deficit at 2.6pc of GDP — the lowest since FY03 for which comparable data is available on the Ministry of Finance website — while the primary surplus reached a historic 2.9pc of GDP. In its annual report on fiscal operations for FY26, the Ministry of Finance reported that petroleum levy collection surged 29pc to Rs1.567tr from Rs1.22tr a year earlier. It also surpassed the original budget target of Rs1.468tr, which had subsequently been revised upward to Rs1.498tr as part of the FY27 budget exercise. The Rs1.567tr petroleum levy did not include an undisclosed amount of customs duty and Rs26bn collected through the carbon levy. For the current fiscal year, the government is targeting an even higher Rs1.676tr in petroleum levy, besides Rs50bn through the climate levy on petroleum products. Despite restructuring and austerity policies, expenditure on running the civil government increased by 16pc to Rs1.033tr from Rs892bn in FY25, breaching the Rs1tr mark for the first time and exceeding the Rs971bn budget estimate. Defence expenditure also increased by 18pc to Rs2.588tr from Rs2.194tr a year earlier. How­ever, it was only Rs38bn higher than the Rs2.55tr budget allocation despite additional requirements following Indian attacks. Total revenue collection declined marginally to 15.6pc of GDP in FY26 from 15.7pc a year earlier. Federal Board of Revenue collection stood at Rs13.01tr, around 10pc short of target but almost 11pc higher than Rs11.74tr collected in FY25. Despite the revenue shortfall, historically high provincial cash surpluses and a steep decline in interest payments enabled the government to sharply reduce the overall fiscal deficit. The primary surplus — the difference between total revenues and expenditure excluding debt servicing — reached 2.9pc of GDP, the highest since the government began reporting the indicator in FY20. The fiscal deficit had peaked at 8.9pc of GDP in FY19 before falling to 8.1pc and 7.1pc in the following two years. It rose again to 7.9pc in FY22 but has since declined amid successive IMF-backed fiscal tightening. Meanwhile, the primary account remained in deficit until turning into a surplus of 0.9pc of GDP in FY24. It improved to 2.4pc the following year and further to 2.9pc in FY26. Three major contributors to the fiscal improvement were record provincial cash surpluses of Rs1.45tr, petroleum levy collection of Rs1.567tr and a Rs1.939tr decline in interest payments. The finance ministry reported that interest payments fell to Rs6.947tr, or 5.5pc of GDP, from Rs8.887tr, or 7.7pc of GDP, in FY2024-25 — a dec­line equivalent to 2.2pc of GDP in a single year. Subsidies were also contained at Rs1.01tr, almost 22pc below Rs1.3tr in FY25, while development expenditure fell to Rs727bn from Rs786bn. Mainly because of savings on interest payments following the easing of the policy rate from 22pc to 10pc, total expenditure declined to Rs23.09tr from Rs24.16tr in FY25. As a result, total expenditure fell to 18.2pc of GDP from 21.1pc a year earlier. Current expenditure also declined to 16.3pc of GDP (Rs20.69tr) from 18.8pc (Rs21.5tr) in FY25. Defence expenditure, however, edged up to 2pc of GDP from 1.9pc. The four provinces posted a 57pc increase in their combined cash surplus to the Centre, taking it to a record Rs1.45tr from Rs921bn in FY25 — an increase of Rs529bn in a single year. They had committed a surplus of Rs1.38tr under the national fiscal pact. Punjab alone provided Rs915bn — almost equivalent to the combined Rs921bn surplus of all four provinces a year earlier and 163pc higher than its Rs348bn contribution in FY25. Sindh followed with a 24pc increase in its surplus to Rs350bn from Rs283bn. PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provided Rs165bn, around 6pc lower than Rs176bn in FY25, while Balochistan posted a surplus of just Rs20.74bn. On the accounting side, the government reported a record statistical discrepancy of Rs853bn. The discrepancy stood at Rs329bn in FY25 and had drawn concern from the IMF, which had suggested a technical mission that the government declined. The finance ministry attributed Rs448bn of the discrepancy to under-reporting at the federal level and Rs405bn to provinces. It said the federal discrepancy stemmed from “variations on account of time lag in reporting and book adjustments amongst SBP, FBR and EAD data”. At the provincial level, Rs266bn of the discrepancy was attributed to increases in commercial bank deposits, while KP and Balochistan accou­nted for Rs95bn and Rs72bn, respectively, also largely due to movements in bank deposits. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: Taliban support
items.description: THE latest UN monitoring report analysing the activities of several transnational terrorist groups is unequivocal in its assessment: the Afghan Taliban “have continued their support” to the banned TTP. Though the report says that the regime in Kabul has taken some tepid steps to control its TTP comrades, this is clearly not enough, as the continuing reign of terror orchestrated by the TTP in Pakistan shows. Moreover, the document also confirms that Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remains a safe haven for a number of lethal terrorist groups, posing a grave security challenge to regional countries. These outfits include IS-K, Al Qaeda — which includes AQIS, its Indian subcontinent arm — and ETIM. The report says that IS-K poses the biggest threat to both the Taliban regime and the broader region, despite suffering setbacks due to the kinetic action taken by Pakistan as well as Kabul. Some parts of the report deserve particular attention. For example, it says that IS-K and the banned BLA may be collaborating. Moreover, the TTP has apparently expanded its operations to Balochistan, Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. Al Qaeda has also solidified its support to the TTP, while AQIS, through the Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan, has stepped up its terrorist attacks in this country. Beyond Pakistan-centric groups, ETIM is active in the Wakhan corridor, which poses a direct threat to China. These findings indicate that the TTP is looking to broaden its geographical reach, while AQIS is also expanding its violent footprint. The UN report says that the Kabul regime has taken some steps to try and control the TTP. These include relocating around 2,000 terrorists and their dependants away from the Pakistan border. Moreover, it says that Afghan Taliban supremo Mullah Hibatullah Akhundzada has “warned the TTP leadership … to halt attacks targeting Pakistan” or risk losing the Taliban’s support. These warnings appear to have fallen on deaf ears, as the TTP has not scaled back its bloody campaign. The fact is that ending the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan will take more than cosmetic steps and lukewarm warnings. If the Taliban regime wants to be taken seriously it needs to take across-the-board action against all terrorist groups on Afghan soil. They cannot pick and choose — for example, fighting IS-K but facilitating the TTP and AQIS. As we have argued earlier on these pages, a multilateral approach is required to address Afghanistan’s terrorism problem. The groups active on Afghan soil pose a threat to the entire region, not just Pakistan. Therefore, all of Afghanistan’s neighbours must send the same message to the Taliban: end support for terrorist groups. If they cooperate they can be integrated into the region; if not, the Kabul regime must be shunned by regional states until it changes its ways. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

items.title: WWC 2027: Black Queens keep qualification hopes alive with playoff win over Côte d’Ivoire
items.description: Ghana kept alive their dream of playing at the 2027 Women’s World Cup with a crucial win over Côte d’Ivoire on Thursday. The Black Queens defeated Côte d’Ivoire 2-1 at the Larbi Zaouli Stadium in Casablanca, coming from behind to seal victory in the play-in game. The Ivorians took the lead after just four minutes after they had won a penalty just 50 seconds into the start of the game. Their advantage came after Princess Marfo fouled her marker in the box with Ines Konan scoring from the penalty spot. The Black Queens gained control of the game thereafter and created chances upon chances but were unable to breach the defence of the Ivorians. Despite their spirited efforts, Ghana were unable to draw level before the break as they went into recess trailing. After recess, Stella Nyamekye thought she had elevated the score for Kim Lars Bjorkegren’s side but her goal was ruled out for a foul on the Ivorian goalkeeper. Shortly after the disallowed goal, Princess Marfo drew parity for the Black Queens, heading home the equaliser from a Stella Nyamekye corner. Thirteen minutes later, Josephine Bonsu shot Ghana into the lead from the spot. The Black Queens were given the advantage following a handball situation in the box with Bonsu making no mistake from 12 yards out. Evelyn Badu and Chantelle Boye-Hlorkah all had efforts late in the game kept out by the Ivorian goalkeeper with Cynthia Konlan also making a brilliant save late in the game to keep the score at 2-1. At the end of the 90 minutes, Ghana were 2-1 winners, grabbing one of two spots available for Africa to compete in the FIFA Playoff tournament for the 2027 Women’s World Cup which starts later this year. In the other playoff game, South Africa registered a 2-1 victory over 2024 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) champions Nigeria to book a slot as well.

items.title: Are the Patriot Games Great? No. Are They Fun to Watch?
items.description: How to describe President Trump’s Freedom 250 Patriot Games? The contest, which took place earlier this week, brought students ages 14 to 17 together from across America to answer the question: What if your high-school gym teacher walked headfirst into a pole and was then asked to throw an Olympics with a budget of exactly $6 and three weeks’ notice? Trump boasted when announcing the games that “there will be no men playing in women’s sports,” but after watching almost all of the Patriot Games , I’ve realized he meant that nobody, regardless of gender, would be playing anything recognizable as a sport. When you turn on ESPN’s coverage of the Patriot Games, you see a camera pan slowly over several small American flags stuck into ill-tended grass, while a tune reminiscent of (but legally distinct from) the Olympics theme plays. Welcome to SPIRE Academy, in Geneva, Ohio, where 120 competitors, one boy and one girl from each of the 50 states and … some territories, gathered for the Patriot Games. Are these the best high-school athletes the United States has to offer? In a word, no. Well, is the person representing Massachusetts at least from the state of Massachusetts ? Also no ! Well, does this field of competitors at least look like America? Not the America I remember! But Stephen Miller has been busy. Then what is this? It’s a Trump-produced spectacle, of course! Who chose these contestants? What are they doing at SPIRE Academy, in Geneva, Ohio? And more important, what are these events ? The kids are not the reason that at the end of three days, I feel almost punished for trying to take the Games seriously. I will say that at least the announcers seem to be equally bewildered by what they’re witnessing. Over the course of the games, I notice that their confident proclamations about what is in store for the contestants keep changing from event to event and day to day. Will Victory Hoops (Pop-A-Shot arcade basketball) feature the top-eight or the top-16 contenders? No one seems to know! (It ultimately features the top 16, despite numerous confident announcements and graphics to the contrary.) If you tuned in only to the finale—sorry, the “Freedom Finale”; every aspect of these games has patriotic branding—you might be forgiven for assuming that the Patriot Games leading up to this point had operated on any kind of recognizable human logic. The finale features four contestants competing on an American Ninja Warrior –style course, and the other 116 competitors lined up behind them in patriotic jerseys. They enter the arena to stirring music and dramatic lighting while sparklers blaze. It looks as though things have been running in a professional manner. Someone tuning in just then might imagine that the whole competition featured such standard tests of skill and not events such as Here, Play Dodgeball, and We’ll Give Half of You 30 Points! They have not been watching the Patriot Games like I have. Some elements of the Patriot Games make a minimal amount of sense. The contest, for instance, begins with something called the Presidential Qualifier, with a 100-meter dash, 55-meter hurdles, a Flexed Arm Hang, a Pro Agility Shuttle, a Broad Jump, and a Med Ball Throw. After the Presidential Qualifier comes Dodgeball and Kickball. Each event, as far as I can tell, is worth 60 points. But I could be wrong! The way Dodgeball and Kickball work is that you are divided into six teams (Team Freedom, Team Liberty, Team Valor, Team Honor, Team Unity, and Team Courage, of course!) via snake seeding. Day two offers two of the most spectacular events I have ever seen. Operation Endurance is a military-inspired obstacle course, and everyone is immediately relieved by how much sense it makes. Ropes to climb! An area in which to army-crawl! A jerrican carry! A balance beam! Yes! And you can tell who has won because there is a timer! But then comes … the Varsity Circuit. This is where you can sense things coming off the rails a bit. The event is divided into six stations, each with an activity representing a sport. There are two football stations, where you run through obstacles and then throw a football at a target. There is a volleyball station, where you serve three balls successfully over the net. There is a baseball station, where you whack a ball off a tee and then run the bases. For the soccer station, you kick a ball at a target. And for tennis, the activity is … catching three tennis balls in a row. Catching! That thing you famously do during the sport of tennis! One announcer tries to zhuzh it up a little bit, so we get this amazing description: “They will be stationed about 15 feet away from the tennis-ball launcher. They have to actually receive this, almost like a punt reception, and they have to do that three times.” And while they do this, their families wave signs that say things such as ELIZA IS OUR PATRIOT . Underwhelming as these challenges are, they are also … not that easy for all of the contestants, which means that if you managed to prove your patriotism sufficiently to get selected for the Patriot Games, you’ll most likely win the prize of failing to catch a tennis ball on national television (or at least deep within the bowels of the ESPN app) while the announcer generously remarks that the lights are awfully bright and the volleyball net does seem pretty high. Certainly not a humiliation for you or the president whose idea this was! After the Varsity Circuit and Operation Endurance, we select our top 16, based on total points. Once we reach the top 16, any pretense that this is an open field for competition where anyone can win gets joyfully abandoned. The top-four scorers are all placed on a single team for tug-of-war against the bottom-four scorers, and—you won’t be surprised to hear this!—they win. After this, we have Pop-A-Shot basketball! Yes, the arcade game! “Why can’t they just shoot real basketballs? Isn’t this all being filmed on a basketball court? Isn’t this allegedly an athletic competition?” HUSH! JUST ACCEPT THE PREMISE! THESE ARE PROBABLY THE BEST ATHLETES, AND THESE ARE PROBABLY LOGICAL THINGS FOR THEM TO BE DOING! Look, as someone who has watched Slippery Stairs , a contest in which people try to climb up a slippery stair and some of them fall down and others do not, I understand the power of good announcing to make almost anything seem like a legitimate competition. But the power of good announcing can go only so far, and it cannot do anything when you are watching two students play arcade basketball head-to-head for no discernible reason, and you already know the points will not matter. Trump appears for the Freedom Finale, which has much higher production value than anything that has come before. “I like a lot of finales,” he says. “We’ve got a lot of good finales.” (Did he prepare those remarks?) During the finale, multiple people fall off the Legally–Distinct–From– American Ninja Warrior Race-Course Equipment, allowing their opponents to win. Thrilling! Everyone gets a medal, and the winners get trophies and scholarship checks. Trump stands smiling in the middle of it all. It looks very Soviet, although the Soviets probably would have realized that the tennis-ball catching was too embarrassing to televise. Is this America? No, this is Trump’s America, where everything is made up and the points don’t matter, but our leader still wants you to cheer as if they do. Just don’t tell me these are tests of merit. I watched that Pop-A-Shot basketball! Don’t tell me this is the best we have to offer. And don’t embarrass our high-school students like this. They have enough being thrown at them, between the death lettuce and resurgent measles. The last thing they need is the Patriot Games too.
